title: Consumer AI choice is task-specific and trust is learned through use, while privacy action depends more on knowledge than concern
source_unit: June 2026 weighted survey and embedded choice experiment of US adult AI-assistant users, Jennifer Zou working paper
geography: United States; adult users of AI assistants

observations.period: June 2026; platform awareness, use, and primary choice

denominator.unit: US adult AI-assistant users in the study sample

primary_platform_share.value: ChatGPT 58.2%, Gemini 25.4%, Claude 7.0%, Copilot 4.1%; weighted estimates
primary_platform_share.unit: percent of AI users naming a primary assistant

task_specialization.value: Claude has 33% primary share for coding tasks versus 7% overall; Copilot is more concentrated in work tasks

multihoming.value: about 43% intentionally route different tasks to more than one platform; trial of a second assistant is more common

observations.method: Weighted descriptive survey of AI-assistant users with six task-specific primary-platform questions; the study uses a Prolific sample and external adoption benchmarks for population weighting.
observations.uncertainty: The sample is not platform telemetry or a longitudinal panel; self-reported task routing does not establish actual usage, durable switching, or provider retention.
observations.subgroup: US adult AI-assistant users; platform and task subgroups have separate denominators and uncertainty.
observations.counterinterpretation: A small platform can occupy a valuable task niche without challenging overall market concentration, and reported multihoming can coexist with strong dependence on one default assistant.

denominator.unit: US adult AI-assistant users; trust and privacy measures use item-specific valid respondents

head_to_head_trust.value: Claude ranked above ChatGPT 59%-41% and above Gemini 66%-34% among respondents ranking both

experiential_trust_lift.value: Claude top-three trust was 41% among aware non-users versus 76% among its users
experiential_trust_lift.unit: percent; user versus aware non-user comparison

privacy_concern_and_knowledge.value: over 80% report concern about conversation-data use, roughly 60% do not know whether their assistant trains on conversations, and only 18% have paid for a better-privacy plan

protective_action_predictor.value: knowledge of the training policy is associated with more protective tools than a one-point increase in concern in the study's regression

observations.method: Paired trust-ranking comparisons and weighted regression of a 0-5 protective-tool count; the cross-sectional study does not establish that use caused trust or that knowledge caused action.
observations.uncertainty: Trust, knowledge, concern, and protective tools are self-reported and measured in one survey; the regression explains a modest share of variation and is not a causal privacy-behavior estimate.
observations.subgroup: AI-assistant users and, for some comparisons, aware non-users or respondents with valid trust/policy items.
observations.counterinterpretation: Users who choose a platform may already differ in risk tolerance, task sensitivity, education, or expectations; continued use despite concern may reflect convenience, habit, or lack of alternatives rather than trust.

denominator.unit: US adult AI-assistant users completing six hypothetical plan choices; valid choice observations vary by task

avoid_human_review.unit: dollars per month; estimated willingness to pay to avoid human review of conversations

avoid_sponsored_answers.unit: dollars per month; estimated willingness to pay to avoid sponsored answers

avoid_training_use.unit: dollars per month; estimated willingness to pay to avoid model training on conversations

sensitivity_gradient.value: willingness to pay to avoid human review rises from $9.45 for non-sensitive to $15.24 for highly sensitive tasks

observations.method: Conditional-logit discrete-choice experiment varying price, human review, training use, and sponsored content across six task-based plan choices.
observations.uncertainty: Hypothetical willingness to pay is not a purchase, privacy-protective behavior, or observed provider change; the estimates apply to the study's choice frame and user sample.
observations.subgroup: US adult AI-assistant users; task sensitivity and concern strata are study-defined.
observations.counterinterpretation: Price remains the primary reason in many choices, so privacy preferences may be subordinate to affordability, and stated protection value may not overcome default-platform dependence.

boundary: This record adds task-level platform choice, comparative and experiential trust, privacy knowledge/action, and hypothetical valuation of data-handling features. It does not establish actual platform telemetry, disclosure, privacy loss, durable switching, dependence, wellbeing, productivity, or causal protective behavior.
